anatomy.flutter: class Press is one StatefulWidget composed at build() from Listener -> AnimatedBuilder/Transform.scale -> _FocusRing -> GestureDetector -> FocusableActionDetector -> Semantics -> TapTarget, conditionally skipping the last four when onTap is null (decorative mode).
anatomy.web: There is no wrapping component at all: styles/motion.css declares one @utility rule (`press` — the merged click transition; five earlier per-variant utilities were folded into it) that only sets `transition`/`transform`/`background-color`/`border-color`/`color`/`box-shadow`/`opacity` on `:active`/`[data-pressed]`; the doc's PressSpecimen applies the class name directly to a plain <button>.
anatomy.note: css-native delivery is a class, not a widget, so it cannot own focus/semantics/hit-testing sub-parts the way Press does; the doc page states the consumer supplies the real element (button/a) that carries those parts, which is the correct web pattern for a CSS-only effect.

api.flutter: Press(scale, onTap, behavior, downDuration, upDuration, semanticLabel, focusNode, autofocus, enabled, showFocusRing, focusRadius, minimumTarget, onFocusChange, onHoverChange, link, expanded) — a single widget with 16 named parameters covering feel, focus, semantics and touch target.
api.web: The 'API' is a single class name: press (scale 0.9, 40ms down via `--duration-press-in`, 250ms spring back on `--duration-normal`/`--ease-emphasized`) — no parameters, only the one fixed set of values read from tokens. The former per-variant choice of five utility names was cut to this one name.
api.note: A single utility standing in for Dart named parameters is the expected CSS-utility shape for a delivery:css-native capability, not a missing feature.

states.flutter: _PressState drives rest -> pressed via AnimationController (_down/_release on PointerDownEvent/PointerUp/PointerCancel) and separately exposes hover via onShowHoverHighlight and keyboard focus via onShowFocusHighlight/_focusVisible, each independently observable through onHoverChange/onFocusChange.
states.web: `@utility press` in styles/motion.css also carries background-color/border-color/color/box-shadow/opacity on the same clock: `transition: transform var(--duration-normal) var(--ease-emphasized), ...` and `&:active, &[data-pressed] { transform: scale(0.9); transition-duration: var(--duration-press-in) }`. No focus, no hover, no semantics.
states.note: CLOSED on review. The finding was that this item's meta.ts description promised 'keyboard operation, focus ring, button or link semantics, a 44px minimum target' — the surface of Flutter's Press WIDGET, written onto a web capability that is one CSS utility and supplies none of them. The description now says what the class actually does and names the four things the host element still owns. The squish itself matched all along; what did not match was the sentence describing it.

disabled.flutter: widget.enabled gates GestureDetector.onTap, FocusableActionDetector.enabled and mouseCursor (basic vs click), and is threaded into Semantics(enabled: enabled) so the control is still announced but not focusable/activatable.
disabled.web: The CSS class has no disabled logic of any kind — no `:disabled` selector in styles/motion.css for `press`; disabled behaviour comes entirely from the host element's native `disabled` attribute, which suppresses `:active` and pointer events by default.
disabled.note: Correct for a CSS-only effect layered on a real <button>/<a>: the native disabled attribute already removes interactivity and is announced by the platform, so re-implementing it in the utility would be redundant.

interaction.flutter: _activateFromKeyboard() is wired to both ActivateIntent and ButtonActivateIntent inside FocusableActionDetector.actions, and explicitly calls _controller.forward()/onTap()/_controller.reverse() so Enter and Space always play the identical squish the pointer path plays.
interaction.web: The `press` utility in styles/motion.css answers `[data-pressed]` beside `:active` with the same transform over the same tokens. Pointer presses arrive through `:active`; keyboard presses arrive through the attribute, which the host sets on keydown of Space/Enter and clears on keyup/blur — the press page's keyboard demo is that host and nothing more.
interaction.note: CLOSED on review, building on the earlier measurement: the class now compensates on its own terms. The remaining difference is the signal — Flutter's GestureDetector and Focus report key-down to the widget, the web reports it to the host through an event the stylesheet cannot see — so a web host has to set one attribute. The demo went from an inline-style re-implementation to wearing `press` with three handlers, which is what a consumer copies. Pinned by e2e/gaps-interaction.spec.ts: focus the demo, hold Space, `transform` is a matrix rather than `none`. ORIGINAL: MEASURED by this worker; verdict stays gap on purpose (see below) rather than being relabelled. On /design-system/components/press (dev server, http://localhost:3111): a real `<button class="press">` was focused and held with a keyboard Space via the browser's own key-press action (not a synthetic KeyboardEvent), with a keydown listener reading `getComputedStyle(button).transform` synchronously, on the next microtask (setTimeout 0) and on the next animation frame. All three reads were `"none"` — Chromium does not apply `:active` for a keyboard Space press on this button at all, in this environment; the audit's own 'inconsistent, browser to browser' framing undersold it; it was consistently absent across every read taken. This does not flip the verdict to match, because `press` itself still does nothing to compensate — per the brief's own instruction, the gap is closed by adding a `[data-pressed]` demonstration rather than by relabelling a capability that still does not do this on its own. components/docs/component-docs/press/keyboard-press-demo.tsx (a client companion file per trap 29 — page.tsx stays a plain spec module) now drives a `data-pressed` attribute from `onKeyDown`/`onKeyUp` on Space and Enter, scaling to the same 0.9 over the same `--duration-press-in` / `--ease-emphasized` tokens `press` itself reads, wired into a new Keyboard section on the doc page — proof the feel can be kept for a keyboard user, and proof it takes a consumer's own script to get there, exactly as Accessibility already says target size and role do. Flutter guarantees the same press feedback for pointer and keyboard; the web class cannot, because :active is not reliably driven by keyboard activation (measured: not driven at all in Chromium), and nothing in this capability compensates for that gap on its own.

semantics.flutter: Semantics(container: true, button: !link, link: link, enabled: enabled, expanded: expanded, label: semanticLabel, onTap: ...) plus TapTarget wrapping to TouchTargets.minimumSize (44x44) via a custom hitTest that forwards off-center taps to the child's centre.
semantics.web: No semantics or hit-area code exists in the class; the Accessibility disclosure instructs using a real button/a element and keeping the target at or above --size-target-min (44px) via padding or an ::after inset, done by the consumer, not the class.
semantics.note: Deferring naming/role/target-size to a real semantic HTML element is the correct web equivalent of Semantics+TapTarget, provided the consumer follows the documented instruction; there is no code enforcement of the 44px floor the way TapTarget enforces it in Flutter, which the doc flags as the consumer's responsibility rather than hiding it.
